titre: A Test That Is 90% Accurate, and Yet Wrong Nine Times Out of Ten
accroche: Faced with a screening test that is 90% reliable, most of the doctors surveyed are completely wrong about the real chance of being ill.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 2007, the German psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer and his colleagues put a question to 160 gynecologists during continuing education: in a population of 40-year-old women with no symptoms, the probability of having breast cancer is 1%. A woman has a mammogram and the result is positive. This test detects 90% of actual cancers, but also gives a positive result in 9% of women who do not have cancer. What is the probability that this woman actually has cancer? Only 21% of the gynecologists surveyed answer correctly. Most put forward a figure close to 90%, or 81%. The right answer is in fact around 9%.

## The Number Almost No One Looks At

The error, known as base rate bias, consists in focusing on the reliability of the test, 90% detection, while forgetting a figure that was nonetheless given in the problem: the rarity of the disease itself. Out of 1,000 women, only 10 actually have cancer (1%); the test detects 9 of them (90% of 10). But among the 990 healthy women, 9% still get a positive result, about 89 women. Of the 98 positive results in all (9 true cases plus 89 false alarms), only 9 are actually ill: 9 divided by 98, or about 9%. The test remains useful, it multiplies the initial 1% probability by nine, but it is very far from pointing to a certainty, because the group of healthy women is huge compared with the group of ill women, and a low false-alarm rate draws a large absolute number of people from it.

## A Problem of Presentation, Not Only of Calculation

Gigerenzer shows that the error is not specific to doctors or to a lack of aptitude for probabilities: it comes largely from the way the problem is worded. Reworded in natural frequencies rather than percentages, out of 1,000 women, 10 have cancer; among them, 9 have a positive test; among the 990 women without cancer, 89 also have a positive test, the same question becomes markedly easier to solve correctly, including for health professionals with no particular statistical training. The consequence goes beyond the case of breast cancer: whenever a screening test, a fraud-detection algorithm, or a security check is applied to a population where the event sought is rare, a positive result remains, most of the time, a false alarm, and mistaking it for a diagnosis amounts to announcing, wrongly, a near-certainty to people who are in reality very probably healthy.

repere.texte: Of 1,000 40-year-old women tested, 10 actually have breast cancer. The test detects 9, but also produces about 89 false alarms among the healthy women: of 98 positive results in all, only 9 correspond to an actual cancer, about 9%, against the 90% or more estimated by the majority of the 160 gynecologists surveyed.
repere.source: Gigerenzer, Gaissmaier, Kurz-Milcke, Schwartz & Woloshin, Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 8(2), 2007

carte.punch: A test that is 90% reliable can be wrong nine times out of ten when it says “positive.”
carte.idee: In 2007, 160 gynecologists answer a simple probability problem: for a disease affecting 1% of women, with a test that is 90% reliable, what is the real probability of being ill after a positive result? Only 21% answer correctly: about 9%, not 90%.

quiz.question: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test detects it in 90% of ill cases, and errs (false positive) in 9% of healthy people. A person tests positive: what is, roughly, their real probability of being ill?
choix: About 90%, since that is the test's announced reliability
About 9%, because the very numerous healthy people produce almost as many false positives as true positives
About 50%, a positive result splitting the probability evenly between ill and healthy
About 99%, by multiplying the test's reliability by the complement of the false-positive rate
quiz.explication: Out of 1,000 people, only 10 are ill (1%) and the test detects 9. But among the 990 healthy people, 9% still get a positive result, about 89 people. Of 98 positive results, only 9 are actually ill: about 9%, not 90%.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What proportion of the 160 gynecologists surveyed by Gigerenzer answers correctly, and what does the majority answer instead?
choix: 21% are wrong, but 79% give the right answer of about 9%
All 160 gynecologists are wrong, with none coming close to the right answer
Only 21% answer correctly; the majority put forward a figure close to 90% or 81%
50% answer correctly, the other half putting forward a figure close to 50%
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Of the 160 gynecologists surveyed by Gigerenzer in 2007, only 21% give the right answer, around 9%. Most put forward a figure close to the test's reliability itself, 90% or 81%, forgetting the rarity of the disease.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What rewording does Gigerenzer show can make the same problem markedly easier to solve correctly?
choix: Giving the doctors a calculator during the test, without changing the problem
Reducing the number of women tested in the problem, from 1,000 to only 100
Replacing breast cancer with an even rarer disease in the problem
Rewording the problem in natural frequencies rather than percentages
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Reworded in natural frequencies, out of 1,000 women, 10 have cancer, among them 9 have a positive test, among the 990 without cancer 89 also have a positive test, the same question becomes markedly easier to solve, including without statistical training.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Beyond cancer screening, to what other fields does the text extend this same reasoning about false positives?
choix: Only to other cancers, never to fields outside medicine
To any screening, fraud detection, or security check applied to a rare event
Only to university statistics exams, with no real practical application
Exclusively to prenatal genetic tests, to the exclusion of any other screening
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text extends the finding beyond breast cancer: whenever a screening test, a fraud-detection algorithm, or a security check is applied to a population where the event sought is rare, a positive result most often remains a false alarm.
